narrative: A Syrian man who had already fled to a refugee camp in Turkey a year earlier, crossing in a rubber raft, then reached Athens, tried about a dozen times to get out of Greece - sneaking toward the Albanian border or trying to fly out on borrowed passports - before the 27-day trek from Athens to Berlin. The most dangerous moment was crossing from Greece into Macedonia, a no-man's land controlled by armed gangs, where he felt eyes in the trees counting his steps; friends who had crossed three days earlier had been attacked and beaten. He agreed to accompany an older Syrian woman of 66, her two daughters and her eldest daughter's fiancee, at times carrying the older woman on his back over rough terrain because she reminded him of his mother and sister. At a hotel near the Macedonian border, about 150 men, women and children gathered to cross; he warned the young men to arm themselves. They began walking under cover of darkness. Around 4 a.m. a small armed group stepped out of the woods, then two larger gangs began circling them. As the group's informal leader he shouted and threatened to hang the attackers from the trees, and the men vanished; the group ran until they reached the Macedonian border, where they were sent back again. By day ten they sheltered at a mosque about ten kilometers from the Serbian border. Three times they tried secret crossing points and were turned back by Serb soldiers; on the fourth he risked a bolder route near the main road, walking and crawling past officials so close he could overhear them, telling his 66-year-old companion, 'Today you will sleep in Serbia.' Without GPS or a map they reached a Serbian village where, by law, Syrians are not returned to Macedonia. From there they continued on foot, by bus and once by taxi - a driver who risked a heavy fine - through Serbia, Hungary and Austria, reaching Berlin on July 5. He felt born again stepping off the bus, saying all the bad things were finished and the good things would start. His oldest childhood friend was waiting at the station, and strangers smiled, knowing they were Syrians by the way they hugged and cried. He later guided four friends along the same route, sharing the map step by step.
